title: Turn and Talk: Powerful, But Not Perfect
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele writes from inside a school that has made 'total participation - every student, every time' a whole-school expectation, with turn and talk as the mandated vehicle. He is a genuine advocate: he picked the routine up from Peps Mccrea's Great Teaching Unpacked, has had positive lesson-observation feedback on it, and believes it was part of why the school adopted it. The piece's value is that it then catalogues the failure modes honestly - silent pairs, friendship dynamics the teacher cannot see, off-task chat between friends, and whole-class flatness that turns the routine into dead time and invites misbehaviour. His sharpest objection is to the seating-plan expectation: leaders require pairs chosen as 'good talking partners', but personality, confidence and willingness to engage are not predictable in September and behaviour data is the only proxy available. His own protocol is to seat by behaviour and character rather than friendship, run the routine two or three times a lesson, and abandon it for another strategy if engagement stays weak - an admitted point of tension with school expectations. The record is worth keeping as a practitioner's account of what happens when a research-backed routine meets a compliance-style mandate.
points: The piece names a real cost of mandated routines: when participation breaks down, a strategy designed to guarantee every student a voice becomes dead time that disrupts pace and invites misbehaviour.

Emanuele's seating-plan critique is the most transferable point - schools require pairs chosen as 'good talking partners' without any reliable way to judge what makes a pair good, especially early in the year.
His working rule is to seat by behaviour and character rather than friendship, and to deliberately push students to talk to people they do not already know well.
He gives himself a stopping rule: two or three attempts at the routine per lesson, then move on - and he is explicit that this collides with the school's expectation.
The one concession he records regretting is granting a student's request to sit with a friend, which he offers as evidence that friendship-based pairing degrades the routine.
quotes: At its simplest, turn and talk means that students pause, turn to their partner, and explain or discuss something for 20–30 seconds. The focus can vary — repeating what I’ve just explained on the board, predicting the next step, or answering a quick check-for-understanding question.

The benefits are clear: it gets every student rehearsing their thinking, it strengthens memory through retrieval and articulation, and it builds confidence in speaking before answering in front of the whole class. It also helps in being a brilliant talking partner.

The seating plan dilemma: My school expects us to set seating plans with “good talking partners” in mind. But how can we really know what makes a good pair? Behaviour is one clue (and we have data), but personality, confidence, and willingness to engage are harder to predict, especially in September.

If participation is low, I don’t give up immediately. I try the routine 2-3 times every lesson. But if after the second/third attempt engagement is still weak, I’ll move on to another strategy to keep the lesson flowing.
Turn and talk is powerful. It’s designed to give every student a voice, to support total participation, and to improve retention. But it only works if students actually do it.

These are the questions that keep me experimenting with this practice. I see the value, I believe in the principle, but I also see the flaws and the stress it can place on teachers when it doesn’t go as planned.
